subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage: Note from Raghav's mother, Rekha. I watched my son's room-cleaning trick tonight. He set the kitchen timer to ten minutes and announced, "Yesterday I took eleven. Today I beat it." He said to me, "If it's a race, I don't get bored. I just keep going." The timer ticked, and he threw clothes into the basket, stacked books, and slid the toys into the box. He was breathing hard and grinning when the bell rang, with one minute left over. I had not asked him to hurry, only to tidy. Turning it into a game was his own idea.

qa.q: How long did Raghav set the timer for?
qa.a: Raghav set the timer for ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Raghav think about turning the chore into a race?
qa.a: Raghav thinks a race keeps him from getting bored so he can keep going, which shows he enjoys the challenge. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Raghav use if racing stops being fun, and why?
qa.a: Raghav could play a favourite song and finish before it ends, or split the room into small jobs. A new challenge would keep his attention on the job.

qa.q: How does Rekha see her son's method?
qa.a: Rekha had only asked him to tidy, so she sees a child who found his own way and is pleased and a little surprised.

grounding: A boy sets a ten-minute timer and tries to beat yesterday's time, making the chore a race so he stays focused and has fun.

subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday
I hate tidying my desk. So today I tried a trick. I set the kitchen timer for ten minutes and said, 'Beat yesterday.' Yesterday it took me fourteen minutes of moaning. Today I made it a race: pens in the jar, books stacked big to small, papers in the tray, crumbs in the bin. I was so busy watching the timer that I forgot to be bored. Eight minutes, forty seconds! Aai said, 'Chaitanya beta, are you feeling well?' Tenzin phoned and I told him my time. He says he'll race me tomorrow with his room. Game on.

qa.q: How long did tidying take yesterday?
Why did Chaitanya forget to be bored?
qa.a: He was so focused and excited about beating the timer that the chore felt like a game 🎉

qa.q: What could keep the race fun after a few days?
qa.a: Racing Tenzin, or setting a new target, so there's always something to beat; the race is what keeps his attention on the job.

qa.q: How does Aai react to the tidy desk?
qa.a: Aai jokes 'are you feeling well?', so she seems surprised and amused by the quick tidying.

grounding: Shows a boy setting a ten-minute timer to beat yesterday's time, turning a boring chore into a race that holds his attention.

subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage: Every evening Pranav had to sweep the courtyard of their village house, and every evening it took forever, because he kept stopping to watch the goats. On Wednesday he had an idea. If it's a race, I won't have time to be bored. 'Vaibhav, watch the clock. Ten minutes. Yesterday it was fifteen. I'm going to beat it.' Vaibhav squatted by the old wall clock. Pranav swept like a cyclone: neem leaves into one pile, dust out through the gate, the corner behind the water drum last. He didn't look at the goats once. 'Nine minutes!' Vaibhav shouted. Pranav leaned on the broom, panting and grinning. 'Tomorrow, eight.'

qa.q: Where did Vaibhav squat to keep time?
How did Pranav feel when Vaibhav shouted 'Nine minutes!'?
qa.a: He was panting and grinning, so he felt proud and excited to have beaten yesterday's time.

qa.q: What else could Pranav race against?
qa.a: His own best time each day, or Vaibhav on another chore; the race keeps his attention off the goats.

qa.q: What is the race like for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav gets the job of timekeeper and shouts the result, so he seems to enjoy being part of it.

grounding: Illustrates a boy turning sweeping into a race against a ten-minute target to beat the day before, which keeps his attention on the chore.
